sections.title: Forty-two seconds late
sections.intro_md:
In the year to March 2019, the average Tokaido Shinkansen train ran 0.7 minutes behind schedule. That figure includes typhoons, snow and earthquakes. When a commuter train in Japan runs about five minutes late, the conductor apologises over the speakers, and the railway will hand you a printed *delay certificate* to show your boss. At Tokyo Station, cleaning crews bow to each arriving bullet train, then turn it round in about seven minutes.

The same country makes pottery older than farming, rebuilds its holiest shrine from scratch every 20 years, prints the world's most copied wave on its banknotes, and now records about 918,000 more deaths than births every year.

Today is a long walk through all of it: 14,000 islands on four tectonic plates, 16,000 years of history, three scripts, two religions practised at once, a cuisine on UNESCO's list, and a country that taught India to build cars and is now teaching it to build bullet trains.

spotlights.name: The Shinkansen
spotlights.spot_it: A long white duck-billed nose, a blue stripe, and a train that arrives at the platform marker to the centimetre.
spotlights.story_md: The first line, Tokyo to Shin-Osaka, opened on **1 October 1964**, nine days before the Tokyo Olympics. It reached 100 million passengers within three years, and the Tokaido line alone has now carried more than **6.5 billion** people. The network runs about **2,951 km** at up to 320 km/h. The long noses are not decoration: they cut the 'tunnel boom', a shock wave that shot out of tunnel mouths when blunt trains pushed air ahead of them. No passenger has died in a derailment or collision on a Shinkansen in commercial service.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed the world, six years before Paris or London tried, that rail could beat the aeroplane on mid-distance trips.
spotlights.memory_hook: A train that apologises for 42 seconds.

sections.title: Japan in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Japan is an island country in the north-west Pacific, a little larger than Germany and about one-ninth the size of India, with roughly **123 million** people at the start of 2026. Around three quarters of its land is mountain and forest, so almost everyone lives on the narrow plains along the coasts. Greater Tokyo, with about 37 million people, was long counted as the largest city region on Earth.

It is a constitutional monarchy: Emperor **Naruhito** has reigned since 1 May 2019, but holds no political power. The National Diet makes the laws, and since October 2025 the Prime Minister has been **Sanae Takaichi**, the first woman in the job. The country is divided into 47 prefectures.

By nominal GDP, Japan is the world's fourth-largest economy, about **$4.3 trillion** in 2026 by IMF estimates. It is also the oldest large society ever recorded: almost three in ten people are 65 or over, and women live to an average of 87.

spotlights.name: Nihon, the sun's origin
spotlights.when: Name from the 7th century; flag law 1999
spotlights.spot_it: A plain red disc on white, set a touch off-centre toward the pole on many old versions, exactly centred by law.
spotlights.story_md: The country calls itself **Nihon** or **Nippon**, written 日本: 'sun' plus 'origin'. Seen from China, Japan lay where the sun came up. In 607 Prince Shotoku sent a letter to the Sui emperor that began 'From the Son of Heaven where the sun rises to the Son of Heaven where the sun sets', which reportedly annoyed the emperor. The red-sun flag, **Hinomaru**, was used on ships from 1870 but became the national flag by law only in **1999**. That law fixed the disc at three-fifths of the flag's height, dead centre.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The name and the flag carry the same idea: Japan as the land at the eastern edge, where the day begins.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sun plus origin: 日 + 本.

sections.title: Islands on four plates
sections.intro_md:
Japan is a 3,000 km arc of islands where four tectonic plates meet: the Pacific and Philippine Sea plates dive under the Eurasian and North American (Okhotsk) plates. That grinding built the mountains, the hot springs and more than 100 active volcanoes, and it makes Japan one of the most earthquake-prone places on Earth. By common estimates, about a fifth of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6 or more happen here.

The five main islands run from **Hokkaido** in the cold north, where sea ice reaches the coast in winter, through **Honshu**, the long main island with Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, to **Shikoku** and **Kyushu**, and down to the subtropical **Okinawa** chain, where coral reefs grow. The climate spans snowfields that bury houses to their eaves on the Sea of Japan side and humid summers with typhoons in the south. Rainfall is high, rivers are short and fast, and good flat land is precious.

spotlights.name: Mount Fuji
spotlights.spot_it: A near-perfect snow-capped cone standing alone above lakes and tea fields, visible from Tokyo on clear winter days.
spotlights.story_md: At **3,776 m** Fuji is Japan's highest mountain, and it is an active volcano. Its last eruption, in **1707**, dropped ash on Edo, 100 km away. UNESCO listed it in 2013 not as a natural site but as a cultural one: a place of worship and a source of art, from Hokusai's prints to pilgrim trails. Hundreds of thousands climb it each summer, many overnight to watch the sunrise from the crater rim. Crowding got so bad that Yamanashi prefecture brought in a daily cap of 4,000 climbers and an entry fee in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the single most repeated image of Japan, and a working volcano near 40 million people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three, seven, seven, six: 3,776 m, and still alive.

spotlights.name: Drift ice at Shiretoko
spotlights.spot_it: A white plain of broken ice plates jammed against a rocky coast, with snow-covered mountains behind.
spotlights.story_md: Every winter, ice that forms off the mouth of the Amur river in Russia drifts south across the Sea of Okhotsk and reaches Hokkaido's north-east coast. At about **44° north**, this is the lowest latitude where sea ice reaches a coast in the northern hemisphere. The ice carries plankton, which feeds fish, which feed Steller's sea eagles and seals. The Shiretoko peninsula, whose Ainu name means roughly 'end of the earth', became a UNESCO natural site in 2005 because of this link between sea ice and land life.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how far Japan stretches: sea ice in the north, coral reefs in the south.
spotlights.memory_hook: Siberian ice parks on a Japanese beach.

spotlights.name: The 2011 earthquake and tsunami
spotlights.spot_it: Ships stranded far inland among flattened houses, and a nuclear plant on the coast with blown-out reactor buildings.
spotlights.story_md: At 14:46 on **11 March 2011**, a magnitude 9.0 to 9.1 earthquake struck off Tohoku, the strongest ever measured in Japan. It moved Honshu about 2.4 m east and shifted Earth's axis by several centimetres. Within an hour, a tsunami up to **40 m** high at its peak run-up hit the coast. Nearly 20,000 people died or remain missing. At **Fukushima Daiichi**, the wave knocked out cooling and three reactors melted down. Japan's sea walls, warning systems and nuclear policy were all rebuilt after it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the event that reshaped modern Japan's sense of risk, energy and the sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: Japan moved 2.4 metres in a single afternoon.

sections.title: The oldest society ever
sections.intro_md:
Japan's population peaked at about 128 million around 2008 to 2010 and has fallen every year since. In 2025 the country recorded **671,236 births and 1,589,489 deaths**: a natural loss of about 918,000 people, roughly a city the size of Chandigarh vanishing in a year. The total fertility rate fell to **1.14** children per woman, far below the 2.1 needed to hold steady.

At the other end, **29.4%** of people were 65 or older in 2025. The number of people aged 100 or more passed 100,000 for the first time in 2026. Around 9 million homes, one in seven, stood empty in 2023; Japanese call them *akiya*.

Japan has also long told itself it is one people. That was never quite true. The **Ainu** of Hokkaido and the people of the old **Ryukyu** kingdom in Okinawa have their own languages and histories, and about 2.8% of residents were born abroad in 2024, a share that is rising fast as Japan quietly lets in more workers.

spotlights.name: A nation of centenarians
spotlights.spot_it: Grey-haired shoppers on a covered street of shops selling red underwear, walking sticks and rice crackers.
spotlights.story_md: When Japan began counting in 1963, it had **153** people aged 100 or more. By September 2026 the health ministry counted **107,677**, the first time the number passed 100,000, and nearly nine in ten were women. Each new centenarian used to receive a silver sake cup from the Prime Minister; the gift was downgraded to silver-plated in 2016 to save money. Tokyo's Sugamo shopping street is nicknamed 'Harajuku for grandmas' because its shops cater to the elderly.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Japan is a preview of the age structure much of the world, including parts of India, will reach this century.

spotlights.name: The Ainu
spotlights.spot_it: Robes of woven tree-bark fibre with bold, curling appliqué patterns in navy and white.
spotlights.story_md: The **Ainu** are the indigenous people of Hokkaido, southern Sakhalin and the Kuril islands. Their name means 'human'. They lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, and made robes called *attush* from the inner bark of elm trees. From the Meiji era, Japan took their land and pushed assimilation. The Ainu language has almost no native speakers left. Only in **2019** did a law recognise the Ainu as an indigenous people, and in 2020 the national Ainu museum, **Upopoy**, opened at Shiraoi. Many Hokkaido place names, including Sapporo, come from Ainu words.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It breaks the old myth that Japan is a country of one people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ainu means 'human'.

sections.title: From cord-marked pots to shoguns
sections.intro_md:
People reached the Japanese islands at least 30,000 years ago. From about **14,500 BCE** the **Jomon** hunter-gatherers made some of the oldest pottery in the world. Wet-rice farming and metal arrived from the Korean peninsula with the **Yayoi** culture in the first millennium BCE, and by the 3rd century CE local rulers were buried in huge keyhole-shaped mounds.

Buddhism and Chinese writing came in the 6th century. Japan copied Tang China's capital plan at **Nara** in 710, then moved to **Heian-kyo**, today's Kyoto, in 794.

Power then slid to the warriors. In 1185 **Minamoto no Yoritomo** set up a military government at Kamakura, and for most of the next 680 years the real ruler was a **shogun**, while the emperor reigned in name. A century of civil war ended with the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, and the Tokugawa shoguns gave Japan 265 years of peace.

spotlights.name: Jomon pottery
spotlights.spot_it: Thick clay pots covered in rope-pressed patterns, some with wild flame-like rims; and goggle-eyed clay figurines.
spotlights.story_md: Shards from the Odai Yamamoto site in Aomori date to around **16,500 years ago**, among the oldest pottery found anywhere. The strange part is who made them: hunter-gatherers, thousands of years before farming reached Japan. Most textbooks link pottery to farming. **Jomon** means 'rope-patterned', from cords pressed into wet clay. Around 3000 BCE potters in Niigata made 'flame-style' vessels whose rims look like fire. The Jomon also made *dogu*, clay figures with huge 'snow goggle' eyes. Jomon sites in northern Japan became a UNESCO site in 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It overturns the idea that settled farming had to come before pottery.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pots before farms, by about ten thousand years.

spotlights.name: Daisen Kofun
spotlights.spot_it: From the air, a giant green keyhole ringed by three moats in the middle of a city; from the ground, just a wooded hill.
spotlights.story_md: The largest of Japan's 'old mounds' is about **486 m** long, longer than the Great Pyramid's base, and covers some 46 hectares with its moats. It was built over about 20 years in the mid-5th century and is traditionally called the tomb of Emperor **Nintoku**, though no one can confirm it. The Imperial Household Agency allows no one inside and no excavation. Clay figures called *haniwa*, of soldiers, horses and houses, once lined such mounds. It joined UNESCO's list in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how powerful Japan's early kings already were, long before written history.
spotlights.memory_hook: A keyhole tomb you can only see from a plane.

spotlights.name: The Great Buddha of Todai-ji
spotlights.spot_it: A dark bronze Buddha 15 m tall with one hand raised, inside a vast wooden hall where tame deer wait outside.
spotlights.story_md: Emperor **Shomu** ordered the Great Buddha in 743, after plague and famine, to hold the country together through faith. It took eight pours of molten bronze over three years and used much of Japan's copper. At the 752 'eye-opening' ceremony before some 10,000 monks, the brush that painted in the pupils was held by **Bodhisena**, a monk from India. Today's hall, rebuilt in 1709 a third smaller than the first, was the world's largest wooden building until 1998. A pillar inside has a hole the size of the Buddha's nostril; children squeeze through it for luck.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It marks Buddhism becoming a state project, and it carries a direct Indian link.
spotlights.memory_hook: An Indian monk painted the eyes of Japan's biggest Buddha.

spotlights.name: The Tale of Genji
spotlights.spot_it: Scroll paintings looking down into court rooms with the roofs removed, full of figures in layered robes.
spotlights.story_md: Around 1008 a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court, known as **Murasaki Shikibu**, was writing a long story about Prince Genji, his loves and the slow sadness of time passing. It runs to 54 chapters and includes about 800 short poems. It is often called the world's first novel. Court men wrote in Chinese; women wrote in the new *kana* script, which is partly why the great prose of the age came from women. The famous 12th-century illustrated scrolls invented a trick called 'blown-off roof' so the viewer can look into the rooms.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the standard for Japanese taste: understatement, seasons, and a feeling for things that pass.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first novel was written by a woman, in a women's script.

spotlights.name: The Mongol invasions and the kamikaze
spotlights.spot_it: A scroll painting of a mounted samurai charging while a bomb bursts in the air beside him.
spotlights.story_md: Kublai Khan, ruler of China, sent fleets against Japan twice. In 1274 the invaders landed at Hakata Bay and fought with exploding ceramic bombs, then withdrew. In **1281** a far larger force came, by some accounts more than 100,000 men. After weeks of fighting, a typhoon wrecked much of the fleet. Japanese called it **kamikaze**, the 'divine wind', and the word came back in 1944 for suicide pilots. A samurai named Takezaki Suenaga had the battles painted on scrolls to prove his bravery and claim a reward, and divers have since found the Mongol wrecks near Takashima.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It created the belief that Japan was protected by the gods, which shaped its thinking for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: A typhoon named 'divine wind' saved Japan twice.

spotlights.name: Sekigahara and the Tokugawa peace
spotlights.spot_it: A painted folding screen packed with banners and mounted armoured soldiers in a valley.
spotlights.story_md: On **21 October 1600**, more than 150,000 samurai met in a foggy valley at Sekigahara. The battle turned when a lord on the western side, **Kobayakawa Hideaki**, switched sides mid-fight. The winner, **Tokugawa Ieyasu**, became shogun in 1603 and ruled from Edo, today's Tokyo. His family then kept power until 1868. They froze society into classes, made lords spend every other year in Edo so they could not plot at home, and kept the country at peace for **265 years**. Samurai became bureaucrats who still wore swords.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It created the stable, inward-looking Japan that the West found in 1853.
spotlights.memory_hook: One lord changed sides and the winner ruled for 265 years.

sections.title: Closed doors, black ships, bombs and booms
sections.intro_md:
From the 1630s the Tokugawa shoguns shut Japan off. Christianity was banned, Japanese could not leave on pain of death, and the only Westerners allowed to trade were the Dutch, on one artificial island in Nagasaki harbour. The policy later got the name *sakoku*, 'closed country'.

In 1853 American warships ended it. Within 15 years the shogunate fell, and the young **Emperor Meiji** was put at the head of a government that copied Western armies, factories, railways and schools at astonishing speed. By 1905 Japan had beaten Russia at war. Its empire then grew into Taiwan, Korea, Manchuria and, after 1937, a war in China and the Pacific that killed millions and ended with atomic bombs on **Hiroshima** and **Nagasaki** and surrender on 2 September 1945.

Under American occupation Japan got a new constitution in 1947 whose **Article 9** renounces war.

spotlights.name: Dejima
spotlights.spot_it: A small fan-shaped island of white warehouses and tiled roofs, now landlocked in the middle of Nagasaki.
spotlights.story_md: In 1634 the shogunate had a fan-shaped artificial island built in Nagasaki harbour, about **120 m by 75 m**, to keep foreign traders away from ordinary people. From 1641 it held the Dutch East India Company, the only Westerners allowed to trade with Japan for more than 200 years. A single bridge linked it to the city, and guards watched it. Through this keyhole Japan imported books on medicine, astronomy and guns, a field of study called *rangaku*, 'Dutch learning'. Land reclamation later swallowed the island, and Nagasaki has rebuilt its houses.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that the 'closed country' was really a country with a filter.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two centuries of Europe through one bridge.

spotlights.name: Perry's black ships
spotlights.spot_it: Japanese woodblock prints of smoking black steamships and a heavy-jowled American officer drawn almost as a demon.
spotlights.story_md: On **8 July 1853**, US Commodore **Matthew Perry** sailed into Edo Bay with four warships, two of them coal-burning steamers belching smoke. The Japanese called them *kurofune*, 'black ships'. Perry delivered a letter demanding that Japan open its ports and said he would return for an answer. He came back in February 1854 with a larger fleet, and in March the shogunate signed the Convention of Kanagawa. Japanese artists rushed out prints of the strangers, some realistic, some monstrous. The humiliation helped bring the shogunate down 14 years later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the shock that started modern Japan.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four black ships, one letter, the end of 250 years of isolation.

spotlights.name: Tomioka Silk Mill
spotlights.spot_it: A long red-brick warehouse with a tiled Japanese roof and wooden framing, a European factory in a farm town.
spotlights.story_md: Four years after the Meiji Restoration, the government built a model silk-reeling factory at **Tomioka**, designed with a French engineer, **Paul Brunat**, and fitted with 300 French reeling machines. Young women from samurai families came to learn the work and took the skills home to start mills of their own. Silk became Japan's biggest export and paid for warships and railways. The mill ran until 1987 and is now a UNESCO site. Many locals at first refused to work there, reportedly because they thought the French were drinking blood. It was red wine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the Meiji strategy: import one model of the best, then copy it everywhere.
spotlights.memory_hook: The French drank 'blood'; it was wine.

spotlights.name: The Atomic Bomb Dome
spotlights.spot_it: A ruined brick building with a bare steel dome frame, standing beside a river in a green park.
spotlights.story_md: The building was finished in 1915 as Hiroshima's Commercial Exhibition hall, designed by a Czech architect, **Jan Letzel**. At 8:15 am on **6 August 1945**, the first atomic bomb used in war exploded about 600 m above and 150 m to the side of it. Because the blast came from almost straight above, some walls stood. Everyone inside died. More than 140,000 people in the city were dead by the end of 1945. A second bomb hit Nagasaki three days later. The ruin was kept as it was and became a UNESCO site in 1996.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the world's clearest monument to what nuclear weapons do.
spotlights.memory_hook: The building survived because the bomb was directly above it.

sections.title: Three scripts in one sentence
sections.intro_md:
Japanese is spoken by about 125 million people and has no proven relatives except the Ryukyuan languages of Okinawa. Its grammar is very unlike Chinese: verbs come at the end, and small particles mark who did what. Yet Japan borrowed Chinese characters to write it, and then had to invent ways to bend them to fit.

The result is the world's most complicated everyday writing system. A single sentence mixes three scripts: **kanji** (Chinese characters for meanings), **hiragana** (curving syllables for grammar endings and native words) and **katakana** (angular syllables for foreign words and emphasis). Signs and computers add the Latin alphabet, called *romaji*. Schools teach 2,136 standard kanji, and newspapers stay mostly inside that list.

Speech is shaped by **keigo**, the honorific system, which changes verbs depending on whether you speak to a boss, a customer or a friend.

spotlights.name: Kana and the Sanskrit order
spotlights.spot_it: Brush calligraphy in black ink on white paper, mixing dense square characters with flowing loops.
spotlights.story_md: The Japanese syllable table, the *gojuon* ('fifty sounds'), runs a, i, u, e, o, then ka, ki, ku, ke, ko, sa, ta, na, ha, ma, ya, ra, wa. That order is not random. It follows the phonetic order of Sanskrit grammarians, learned by Japanese Buddhist monks who studied the **Siddham** script brought from India via China. So every Japanese dictionary and every list of names is ordered on an Indian pattern. Children learn hiragana first, then katakana, then about 1,000 kanji in primary school.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a hidden thread of Indian learning inside everyday Japanese.
spotlights.memory_hook: Japanese dictionaries are in Sanskrit order: a, i, u, e, o.

sections.title: Shinto and Buddhism, both at once
sections.intro_md:
Ask Japanese people their religion and about seven in ten say they have none. Yet most visit a Shinto shrine at New Year, marry in a shrine or a chapel, and are buried with Buddhist rites. The government's count of religious members comes to well over the population, because shrines and temples each count the same households.

**Shinto** is Japan's native faith: the worship of *kami*, spirits that live in mountains, waterfalls, old trees, ancestors and even rice. It has no founder, no single holy book and few rules about belief. Its centres are shrines, marked by a **torii** gate. Japan has around 100,000 of them, about 80,000 under one national association. **Buddhism** arrived from Korea in the 6th century and blended with Shinto for more than a thousand years, until the Meiji government forcibly separated them in 1868 and built 'State Shinto' around the emperor. That ended in 1945. A saying sums up the result: born Shinto, married Christian, die Buddhist.

spotlights.name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
spotlights.spot_it: Tunnels of bright vermilion gates climbing a wooded hill, each post carved with black writing on the back.
spotlights.story_md: This is the head shrine of **Inari**, the kami of rice, and so of prosperity and business. Since 711, worshippers have climbed Mount Inari behind it. Today the trail runs under thousands of vermilion **torii**, often put at around 10,000. Each gate was donated by a company or person, whose name and date are written on it, as a prayer for good business. Stone foxes, Inari's messengers, guard the paths with keys or scrolls in their mouths. Admission is free and the shrine is open all night.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Shinto as a working faith that blesses money, rice and offices, not just mountains.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten thousand gates, each one a company's prayer.

spotlights.name: Ise Jingu, rebuilt every 20 years
spotlights.spot_it: Plain unpainted cypress buildings with thatched roofs and crossed beams at the gables, beside an empty plot of white pebbles.
spotlights.story_md: Japan's holiest shrine, to the sun goddess **Amaterasu**, is torn down and rebuilt on a neighbouring plot every **20 years**. The first rebuilding was in 692. The 62nd was in **2013**, and the next is due in **2033**. The process takes about 17 years, from cutting cypress in sacred forests to the night the goddess is moved. Carpenters pass the skills down from one rebuild to the next. The old wood is reused at other shrines. So a building in a 7th-century design is never more than 20 years old.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a different idea of permanence: keep the knowledge alive, not the material.
spotlights.memory_hook: The oldest shrine is always brand new.

spotlights.name: The floating torii of Itsukushima
spotlights.spot_it: A huge orange gate standing in the sea at high tide, then on wet sand at low tide.
spotlights.story_md: The island of Miyajima was itself held sacred, so commoners were not supposed to step on it. The solution, in its present form from 1168, was to build the shrine on stilts over the water and put its gate in the sea. The present **torii**, about 16 m high, dates from **1875**. It is not buried in the seabed. It stands by its own weight, with stones packed into its top beam. At low tide you can walk out to it. The shrine joined UNESCO's list in 1996.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the 'three views of Japan', and the clearest image of the sacred meeting the sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gate that stands in the sea by its own weight.

sections.title: Masks, makeup, waves and drums
sections.intro_md:
Japan keeps old performing arts alive as living professions, passed from father to son over many generations. **Noh**, the slow masked drama of the 14th century, is the oldest major theatre form still regularly performed anywhere. **Kabuki**, loud, colourful and commercial, was the popular theatre of Edo's merchants. **Bunraku** uses near life-size puppets worked by three handlers in full view. All three are on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

In pictures, the Edo period's great invention was **ukiyo-e**, 'pictures of the floating world', woodblock prints cheap enough for townspeople. They showed actors, courtesans and landscapes. When they reached Europe in the 1860s, often as packing paper, they changed Western art: Monet, Van Gogh and Degas collected them.

Taste across these arts shares a few ideas: *ma*, the meaningful pause or empty space; *wabi-sabi*, beauty in the worn and imperfect; and *mono no aware*, a gentle sadness at things passing.

spotlights.name: Noh
spotlights.spot_it: A masked actor in a stiff brocade robe sliding his feet across a bare cypress stage with a pine tree painted on the back wall.
spotlights.story_md: In the late 14th century an actor named **Kan'ami** and his son **Zeami** won the patronage of the shogun and shaped Noh into its present form. Zeami also wrote the theory of the art, and many of his plays are still performed. Actors glide with a sliding step called *suriashi*. Masks are carved so that a tilt of the head changes the expression: tilted down, a mask seems to cry; tilted up, it seems to smile. Plays often feature ghosts who return to retell their regrets. Noh was among the first arts UNESCO honoured, in 2001.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its slowness and masks influenced modern theatre from Yeats to Peter Brook.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tilt the mask down and it weeps.

spotlights.name: Kabuki
spotlights.spot_it: Actors in red-and-white face paint and huge wigs freezing in crossed-eye poses while the audience shouts their stage names.
spotlights.story_md: Kabuki was started in **1603** by a woman, **Izumo no Okuni**, who danced on a dry riverbed in Kyoto. Its popularity, and the sex trade around it, worried the shogunate, which banned women from the stage in **1629**. Since then all roles are played by men; specialists in female roles are called *onnagata*. Actors inherit stage names over generations, like Ichikawa Danjuro, now in its 13th holder. At the peak of a scene the actor freezes in a *mie* pose and fans shout his house name, timed like a cheer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of a 400-year-old popular art still running as a business.
spotlights.memory_hook: Founded by a woman, played only by men since 1629.

spotlights.name: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
spotlights.spot_it: A giant blue wave curling into claw-like foam over three tiny boats, with snow-capped Fuji small in the trough.
spotlights.story_md: **Katsushika Hokusai** made this woodblock print when he was about 70, as the opening image of a series, *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji*. It was a cheap print, made in thousands. The deep blue is **Prussian blue**, a synthetic pigment newly imported from Europe. Fuji, the largest mountain in Japan, is the smallest thing in the picture. About 100 early impressions survive in museums; the British Museum has compared 111 of them. Debussy put the wave on the cover of *La Mer* in 1905, and since 2024 it is on the back of Japan's 1,000 yen note.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is probably the most reproduced artwork from Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: The mountain is the smallest thing in the picture.

spotlights.name: Taiko drumming
spotlights.spot_it: Barrel drums as big as a car tyre struck with thick sticks by drummers in loincloths and headbands, moving like athletes.
spotlights.story_md: Drums have been used in Japan for at least 1,500 years, in shrines, festivals and on battlefields to signal troops. But the big group performance most people now picture is modern. In **1951** a jazz drummer, **Daihachi Oguchi**, rearranged a shrine piece for a full set of taiko of different sizes, like a drum kit spread across a stage. The style, *kumi-daiko*, spread fast. The group **Kodo**, based on Sado Island, made it world famous from the 1980s. There are now thousands of taiko groups in Japan and abroad.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how 'ancient' traditions are often recent inventions on old roots.
spotlights.memory_hook: A jazz drummer invented 'traditional' taiko in 1951.

sections.title: Made to last, mended to show
sections.intro_md:
Japan treats some craftspeople as national treasures, literally. Since 1955 the state has named **Living National Treasures**, masters of crafts and performing arts who get a stipend to practise and to teach. There are about 100 at a time, in potting, lacquer, dyeing, metalwork, swords, paper and more.

Three crafts show the spirit well. The **sword** is the most refined use of steel in pre-modern history. **Kintsugi** repairs broken pottery with gold instead of hiding the crack. **Washi** paper is so strong and long-lasting that museums around the world use it to mend old paintings and books. Behind them sit shared ideas: respect for the material, years of apprenticeship, and the belief that a thing used and repaired has more value, not less. Craft towns, from Arita porcelain to Kyoto textiles, still often depend on a single family workshop.

spotlights.name: The Japanese sword
spotlights.when: Curved form from about the 10th century
spotlights.spot_it: A slightly curved single-edged blade with a cloudy, wavy line along the edge called the hamon.
spotlights.story_md: Smiths make the sword from *tamahagane*, steel smelted from iron sand in a clay furnace called a *tatara* over three days. They fold and hammer it many times to even out the carbon. Then they coat the blade in clay, thin at the edge and thick on the back, and quench it in water. The edge cools fast and turns very hard; the back stays softer, and the difference makes the blade bend into its curve. The cloudy line where the two meet is the *hamon*. Licensed smiths today are limited to making two long swords a month.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a peak of pre-industrial metallurgy, and its curve comes from physics, not design.
spotlights.memory_hook: The curve is made by cooling, not bending.

spotlights.name: Kintsugi
spotlights.spot_it: A tea bowl crossed by bright gold lines where it was once broken.
spotlights.story_md: Kintsugi, 'golden joinery', repairs broken ceramics with **urushi** lacquer, the sap of the lacquer tree, and then dusts the seams with powdered gold. A popular story says the shogun **Ashikaga Yoshimasa** sent a cracked Chinese tea bowl back to China for repair in the 15th century, got it back stapled with ugly metal clamps, and asked Japanese craftsmen for something better. True or not, the craft grew with the tea ceremony, where an old mended bowl could be worth more than a new perfect one. Real kintsugi takes weeks, because lacquer must cure in humid air.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns damage into part of an object's history instead of something to hide.
spotlights.memory_hook: The crack becomes the gold.

spotlights.name: Washi paper
spotlights.spot_it: Thin, slightly fuzzy paper with long fibres visible when held to the light, glowing in sliding shoji screens.
spotlights.story_md: Washi is made from the inner bark of plants such as *kozo*, a kind of mulberry. Makers steam and beat the fibres, mix them in cold water with a sticky plant extract, and rock a bamboo screen so the long fibres criss-cross. The sheets are thin but very strong, and can last over a thousand years: the oldest dated paper in Japan, from 702, is still in the Shosoin storehouse in Nara. Conservators at museums around the world use washi to repair paintings and books. In 2014 UNESCO listed three washi traditions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why so many old Japanese documents survive, and it helps save Western ones too.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paper from the year 702 is still readable.

sections.title: Washoku: rice, soup and the seasons
sections.intro_md:
In 2013 UNESCO added **washoku**, 'Japanese food', to its intangible heritage list, especially as eaten at New Year. The listing was not about one dish but a way of eating: fresh seasonal ingredients, rice at the centre, a bowl of miso soup, small side dishes, and **umami**, the savoury taste a Tokyo chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, named in 1908 after studying kelp broth. Its base is *dashi*, a stock of kelp and dried bonito flakes.

For 1,200 years, Buddhist rules discouraged eating meat, and the Japanese diet leaned on fish, soy and vegetables. Beef came back only with the Meiji reforms. Much of what the world now calls Japanese food is surprisingly modern: nigiri sushi began as Edo street food, ramen arrived from China around 1900, and instant noodles were invented in a backyard in 1958. Tokyo has held the most Michelin-starred restaurants of any city for years.

spotlights.name: Nigiri sushi
spotlights.spot_it: A thumb-sized ridge of vinegared rice pressed by hand under a slice of raw fish, eaten in one bite.
spotlights.story_md: Sushi began as a way to preserve fish: it was packed in rice and left for months to ferment, and the rice was thrown away. In the 1820s Edo street cooks, traditionally credited to **Hanaya Yohei**, sped this up by seasoning rice with vinegar and pressing fresh fish from Edo Bay on top. It was fast food, sold from stalls. Tuna's fatty belly, now prized as *toro*, was once fed to cats. At the New Year auction in 2019, a 278 kg bluefin tuna sold for **333.6 million yen** at Tokyo's Toyosu market.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a preserving method turned into the world's best-known Japanese food.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sushi began as fish preserved in rice that was thrown away.

spotlights.name: Ramen
spotlights.spot_it: A deep bowl of wheat noodles in rich broth topped with sliced pork, a soft egg, nori and spring onion, slurped loudly.
spotlights.story_md: Ramen came from Chinese wheat-noodle soups brought by Chinese cooks to port cities. **Rairaiken**, which opened in Asakusa in **1910** with Japanese owners and Cantonese cooks, is often called the first ramen shop. After the war, cheap American wheat made noodles a staple. Each region now has its own: miso ramen in Sapporo, creamy pork-bone *tonkotsu* in Hakata, soy-sauce *shoyu* in Tokyo. Slurping is polite; it cools the noodles and shows you are enjoying them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a Chinese dish that became Japan's most popular everyday meal and then a global export.
spotlights.memory_hook: Slurp loudly: it is a compliment.

spotlights.name: The tea ceremony
spotlights.when: Shaped by Sen no Rikyu, 16th century
spotlights.spot_it: A host kneeling on tatami whisking bright green powdered tea in a rough bowl, guests turning the bowl before drinking.
spotlights.story_md: Tea arrived from China with Buddhist monks; the monk **Eisai** brought seeds and powdered-tea methods back in 1191. **Sen no Rikyu** (1522 to 1591) turned serving it into *chado*, 'the way of tea': plain rough bowls, tiny rooms of two tatami mats, and a small crawl-in door so that every guest, even a samurai, had to bow and leave his sword outside. Rikyu served the warlord **Toyotomi Hideyoshi**, who in 1591 ordered him to kill himself, for reasons still argued over. The ceremony he shaped survives through his descendants' schools.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It packed a whole philosophy of simplicity and respect into one bowl of tea.
spotlights.memory_hook: A door so low that even a samurai had to bow.

spotlights.name: Instant noodles
spotlights.spot_it: A paper-and-plastic cup with a peel-back lid; add boiling water, wait three minutes.
spotlights.story_md: **Momofuku Ando** had lost his business and was 48 when he started experimenting in a shed behind his house in Ikeda. He saw long queues for ramen in post-war Osaka and wanted a noodle anyone could make at home. His trick was to flash-fry seasoned noodles, which dried them and left tiny holes that soak up hot water. **Chicken Ramen** went on sale on 25 August 1958. **Cup Noodles**, in a cup that is also the bowl, followed in 1971. He later developed a version for astronauts. The world now eats over a hundred billion servings a year, and India is among the biggest markets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It may be modern Japan's most widely used invention.
spotlights.memory_hook: A broke 48-year-old in a backyard shed fed the world.

sections.title: A year of matsuri
sections.intro_md:
A **matsuri** is a festival, usually tied to a local shrine. Its core is often simple: the shrine's kami is carried around the neighbourhood in a portable shrine, a *mikoshi*, by dozens of chanting bearers, so it can see and bless its people. Around that come floats, food stalls, drums and dancing.

The national calendar adds seasonal days for everyone. New Year, **Shogatsu**, is the biggest: families clean the house, visit a shrine, and eat special boxed food. In spring the whole country watches the cherry-blossom forecast. **Obon** in August welcomes the spirits of ancestors home, and towns dance in circles to greet them. Children have their own days: Girls' Day on 3 March with displays of dolls, Children's Day on 5 May with carp streamers. Snow festivals light up the north in February, and huge lantern floats roll through Aomori in August.

spotlights.name: Hanami
spotlights.spot_it: Blue tarps under clouds of pale pink blossom, office groups picnicking with beer, and petals falling on everyone.
spotlights.story_md: Hanami, 'flower viewing', goes back to Heian court poets. Today the Japan Meteorological Agency watches official 'sample trees', the Tokyo one at Yasukuni Shrine, and declares the season open when five or six flowers open. Most trees are **Somei-Yoshino**, a single clone bred in Edo in the 19th century, so whole regions bloom at once and for only about a week. Kyoto's court diaries let scientists track peak bloom dates back to 812. In **2021** Kyoto's blossoms peaked on 26 March, the earliest in that 1,200-year record, a clear signal of warming.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties Japan's aesthetic of fleeting beauty to one of the longest climate records on Earth.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 1,200-year diary of cherry blossoms caught global warming.

spotlights.name: Gion Matsuri
spotlights.spot_it: Towering wooden floats hung with tapestries, pulled by ropes, with musicians playing flutes and gongs high on top.
spotlights.story_md: Kyoto's great festival began in **869** as a ritual to calm the gods believed to cause a plague. It now fills all of July. The high point is the procession of **yamahoko** floats on 17 and 24 July. The largest weigh about 12 tonnes and rise some 25 m, and they have no steering: at each corner, crews lay split bamboo on the road, wet it, and haul the float round in a slow skid. Some floats are hung with antique tapestries, including a 16th-century Flemish tapestry and Persian and Indian carpets. UNESCO listed the floats in 2009.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a moving museum, and a plague ritual that has run for over 1,150 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve tonnes, no steering, turned on wet bamboo.

spotlights.name: Awa Odori
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of women in straw hats bent like half-moons stepping on tiptoe, men low and loose behind them, all to a shamisen and drum beat.
spotlights.story_md: Japan's biggest Obon dance fills the streets of **Tokushima** on Shikoku for four nights each August and draws more than a million spectators. Groups called *ren* dance through the streets in two styles: women upright and elegant in tilted straw hats, men crouched and loose. The chant explains the spirit: 'The dancers are fools, the watchers are fools. If we are all fools, why not dance?' The festival is said to be about 400 years old, and anyone can join the open groups.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns a festival for the dead into the most joyful street party in Japan.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fools dance, fools watch, so dance.

sections.title: Rules of the room
sections.intro_md:
Life in Japan runs on shared, mostly unspoken rules. Shoes come off at the **genkan**, the step inside the door. You do not eat while walking, talk loudly on trains or tip. Rubbish is sorted into many categories and put out on set days. People queue, and they return lost wallets: Tokyo's police receive billions of yen in lost cash each year, and a large share of it finds its way back to the owners.

Sociologists describe a culture of **group harmony** (*wa*), reading the air (*kuuki wo yomu*, sensing what others want without being told), and a gap between private feeling (*honne*) and public face (*tatemae*). These are tendencies, not laws, and younger Japanese push against many of them. Japanese bow to greet, thank and apologise: about 15° for a passing colleague, 30° for a customer, 45° or deeper for a serious apology.

Work has a hard reputation. The word **karoshi**, 'death from overwork', was coined in the 1970s and the first case was reported in 1969. Laws since 2019 cap overtime, and average working hours per worker have fallen below the OECD average, partly because more people now work part-time.

spotlights.name: Onsen
spotlights.spot_it: A steaming outdoor rock pool among snowy trees, sometimes with red-faced monkeys sitting in it.
spotlights.story_md: Japan's volcanoes heat thousands of hot springs, and **onsen** bathing is a national ritual. The rules: wash and rinse fully at a stool and tap before getting in, enter naked, keep your small towel out of the water (many people fold it on their head), and do not swim. Baths are usually split by sex. Many onsen still bar people with tattoos, a rule linked to the *yakuza*, though some now welcome foreigners with small ones. In Jigokudani in Nagano, wild Japanese macaques bathe in a hot pool in winter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Japanese bathing as social and restful, not only about getting clean.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wash first, soak second, towel on your head.

spotlights.name: Vending machines everywhere
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of glowing machines on a quiet street at night, selling hot and cold drinks side by side.
spotlights.story_md: Japan has one vending machine for roughly every 23 people, the highest density in the world. Most sell drinks, but there are machines for hot meals, umbrellas, eggs, toilet paper, SIM cards and fresh flowers. They are rarely vandalised, which is part of why they work outdoors in quiet streets. Some machines double as emergency supply points: after a big earthquake they can be switched to give out drinks for free, and some carry disaster information displays.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They reflect low crime, high labour costs and a love of convenience.
spotlights.memory_hook: One machine for every 23 people.

sections.title: Exports of the imagination
sections.intro_md:
After the war, Japan's most powerful export, after its cars and electronics, turned out to be its imagination. **Akira Kurosawa**'s *Rashomon* won at Venice in 1951 and *Seven Samurai* (1954) was remade in Hollywood as *The Magnificent Seven*. **Godzilla** rose from Tokyo Bay in 1954 as a walking metaphor for the atomic bomb. **Manga** and **anime** grew from Osamu Tezuka's *Astro Boy* into an industry that now shapes children's imaginations worldwide, from *Dragon Ball* to *Naruto* and *Demon Slayer*.

Games came next. Nintendo, Sony's PlayStation and Sega turned a small country into a superpower of play. Then came characters, *kawaii* (cute) culture, karaoke, emoji (the word is Japanese: 'picture' plus 'character') and, lately, J-pop city pop on streaming playlists.

Sport shows another face: centuries-old **sumo** next to modern baseball, Japan's most popular team sport, which produced the most famous Japanese athlete alive.

spotlights.name: Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli
spotlights.spot_it: Hand-drawn films of flying machines, forest spirits, girls on brooms and huge grey fuzzy creatures at bus stops.
spotlights.story_md: **Hayao Miyazaki** co-founded Studio Ghibli in **1985** and still insists on hand drawing. *My Neighbour Totoro* (1988) gave the studio its logo. *Spirited Away* (2001) became the highest-grossing film in Japanese history for 19 years and in 2003 won the Oscar for best animated feature, the first non-English film to do so. He has 'retired' several times; *The Boy and the Heron* won him a second Oscar in 2024 at 83. His films are full of strong girls, flight, war's cost and respect for nature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He proved animation can be art for adults as well as children, without computers or happy endings.
spotlights.memory_hook: A forest spirit at a bus stop won Japan its first animation Oscar.

spotlights.name: Nintendo
spotlights.spot_it: A red oval logo; a plumber in red cap and blue overalls; small playing cards with bright pictures of flowers.
spotlights.story_md: Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in **1889** by **Fusajiro Yamauchi** to make *hanafuda*, flower-pattern playing cards. In the 1960s it tried taxis, instant rice and 'love hotels' before toys took off. The **Famicom** (1983, sold abroad as the NES) and **Shigeru Miyamoto**'s *Super Mario Bros.* (1985) rebuilt the video-game business after the American crash of 1983. Later came the Game Boy, Pokemon, the Wii and the Switch. The **Switch 2**, launched on 5 June 2025, sold 3.5 million units in its first four days, a record for a Nintendo machine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a 137-year-old company that keeps surviving by inventing new ways to play.
spotlights.memory_hook: A playing-card company from 1889 made Mario.

spotlights.name: Shohei Ohtani
spotlights.spot_it: A tall player who both pitches and bats at the top level, something baseball had not seen since Babe Ruth a century ago.
spotlights.story_md: **Shohei Ohtani** from Iwate both pitches and hits in Major League Baseball, a double role thought impossible in the modern game. In December 2023 he signed a 10-year, **$700 million** contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers, then the largest in sports history. In 2024 he became the first player ever with **50 home runs and 50 stolen bases** in a season. He won the World Series in 2024 and 2025 and his fourth Most Valuable Player award in 2025. In Japan, his games are shown live at breakfast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the most famous Japanese person alive and a symbol of Japan winning on American terms.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two players in one body: he pitches and he hits.

spotlights.name: Sumo
spotlights.spot_it: Two huge wrestlers in silk belts crouching in a clay ring, throwing handfuls of salt before they charge.
spotlights.story_md: Sumo grew out of Shinto ritual and still looks like it. A roof shaped like a shrine hangs over the ring, the referee dresses like a court official, and wrestlers throw salt to purify the clay. The rules are simple: push your opponent out of the **4.55 m** ring or make him touch the ground with anything but his feet. Wrestlers live in communal 'stables', wear their hair in topknots and eat a stew called *chanko*. The top rank is **yokozuna**; in 2025 Japan got two new ones, Hoshoryu, born in Mongolia, and Onosato, born in Ishikawa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living link between Shinto ritual and modern professional sport.
spotlights.memory_hook: Salt in the ring, a shrine roof above it.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Japan received a record **42.7 million** foreign visitors in 2025, and most of them crowded into the same 'golden route': Tokyo, Mount Fuji, Kyoto and Osaka. That route is popular for good reason. Kyoto, spared from heavy bombing in the war, holds 17 sites in a single UNESCO listing and around 1,600 temples. Nara, the capital before it, has the Great Buddha and more than a thousand tame deer that bow for crackers.

But the country rewards anyone who leaves the route. Hokkaido has powder snow and drift ice. The Japan Alps have villages of steep thatched farmhouses at **Shirakawa-go**. Hiroshima and the floating torii of Miyajima make one day trip. The island of **Naoshima** is filled with modern art. **Yakushima**, in the south, has cedar trees thought to be thousands of years old. And Okinawa's islands have their own Ryukyu culture, food and music.

spotlights.name: Shibuya Crossing
spotlights.native_name: 渋谷スクランブル交差点
spotlights.spot_it: Giant video screens, a five-way scramble crossing and a wave of people that pours out from every corner when the lights all turn green.
spotlights.story_md: Outside Shibuya Station, traffic stops in every direction at once and pedestrians cross from all sides, including diagonally. At busy times well over a thousand people, by some counts up to 3,000, cross on a single green light, without collisions. It is often called the world's busiest pedestrian crossing. The best views are from the station's upper floors and the Shibuya Sky deck. The station's best-known meeting point is the bronze statue of **Hachiko**, a dog whose story you will meet later today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most filmed image of modern Tokyo's density and order.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thousands cross at once, and nobody bumps.

spotlights.name: Himeji Castle
spotlights.spot_it: A tall white castle of stacked curving roofs on a stone base, often called the White Heron.
spotlights.story_md: Himeji is the finest of Japan's 12 castles whose original keeps survive. It was completed in **1609** under the lord Ikeda Terumasa, with white plaster walls that protect the wooden frame from fire and a maze of gates and dead-end paths built to confuse attackers. It survived the end of the samurai, firebombing in 1945 that burned most of the city around it, and the 1995 Kobe earthquake. In 1993 it was among the first four places in Japan to join the UNESCO list. A five-year restoration ended in 2015.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best surviving example of how samurai built for war and for show at the same time.
spotlights.memory_hook: The white heron survived bombs and an earthquake.

spotlights.name: Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion
spotlights.spot_it: A three-storey pavilion covered in gold leaf, mirrored in a still pond with pine islands.
spotlights.story_md: The shogun **Ashikaga Yoshimitsu** built this as his retirement villa in 1397, and after his death it became a Zen temple. The top two floors are covered in gold leaf. It survived wars for over 500 years, then in **1950** a 22-year-old trainee monk set fire to it and burned it to the ground. The writer **Yukio Mishima** turned the arson into a famous novel in 1956. What visitors see today is a 1955 reconstruction, re-gilded with thicker gold leaf in 1987.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a building can be both a 600-year-old design and a post-war copy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A monk burned it, a novelist immortalised it.

sections.title: How Japan earns
sections.intro_md:
Japan rebuilt from defeat into the world's second-largest economy by 1968, a place it held until China passed it in 2010.

In the late 1980s, land and share prices went mad: by one famous estimate, the grounds of the Imperial Palace in Tokyo were worth as much as all the land in California. The **Nikkei** index peaked at 38,915 on 29 December 1989. Then the bubble burst. Prices fell for years, and the index did not pass that peak again until **February 2024**, 34 years later.

Today Japan is the world's fourth-largest economy in nominal terms, behind the US, China and Germany, with India close behind or level. Its public debt is about **230% of GDP**, the highest of any rich country, but most is owed to Japanese savers. Unemployment is low, near 2.5%. Cars are still the biggest export, and inbound tourism has become one of the largest earners.

spotlights.name: Toyota and just-in-time
spotlights.spot_it: A factory line where any worker can pull a cord to stop production, and parts arrive in small bins exactly when needed.
spotlights.story_md: Toyota began inside a loom company. **Sakichi Toyoda** built an automatic loom that stopped itself when a thread broke, so one worker could watch many machines. His son **Kiichiro** started making cars in 1937. After the war, engineer **Taiichi Ohno** built the **Toyota Production System**: *just-in-time* delivery of parts, inspired partly by how American supermarkets restock shelves; *kanban* cards that signal what to make next; and the right of any worker to stop the line to fix a fault. Toyota has been the world's best-selling carmaker by volume for several years running.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its methods, renamed 'lean', changed how factories, hospitals and software teams work worldwide.
spotlights.memory_hook: Any worker can stop the line.

spotlights.name: Kongo Gumi and the shinise
spotlights.spot_it: A red-and-white five-storey pagoda in Osaka, rebuilt again and again by the same family of carpenters.
spotlights.story_md: In **578**, a carpenter named **Shigemitsu Kongo** came from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build Shitenno-ji, one of Japan's first Buddhist temples. His family's firm, **Kongo Gumi**, kept rebuilding that temple and others for more than 1,400 years, through 40 generations. In 2006, hurt by debts from the 1980s bubble, its business was taken over by a larger builder, which still runs it. Japan has more companies over 100 years old than any other country, tens of thousands of them, called *shinise*, including a hot-spring inn open since 705.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a business culture that values survival and craft over fast growth.
spotlights.memory_hook: A family firm that lasted 1,428 years.

sections.title: Japan and India
sections.intro_md:
The link between India and Japan is older than most people think, and it runs through Buddhism. The religion reached Japan from India by way of China and Korea, and the Japanese came to call India *Tenjiku*, 'heaven's centre'. In 736 an Indian monk arrived in Nara and stayed for life.

In modern times, the link ran through art and revolution. Okakura Kakuzo and Rabindranath Tagore shaped each other's ideas of Asia. Indian revolutionaries sheltered in Tokyo, and the Indian National Army fought beside Japan in the Second World War. After the war, India's judge at the Tokyo trials became a hero to Japanese nationalists, and India gave up all claims to war reparations when it signed a separate peace treaty in 1952.

Since the 1980s, the link runs through money and machines: cars, the Delhi Metro, and now a bullet train. India has been the largest recipient of Japanese development aid for years, and the two governments now call each other 'special strategic and global partners'. Japan pledged in 2025 to roughly double private investment in India over the next decade.

spotlights.name: Bodhisena
spotlights.spot_it: A South Indian monk in Nara-period robes, remembered at Todai-ji every year on the anniversary of the eye-opening.
spotlights.story_md: **Bodhisena** was a Buddhist monk from India who travelled to China and then, at the invitation of Emperor Shomu, reached Japan in **736**. He taught Sanskrit in Nara and, in **752**, led the ceremony that 'opened the eyes' of the Great Buddha at Todai-ji, painting in the pupils with a giant brush. Colourful cords tied to the brush ran out to the crowd so that thousands of people could touch them and share the merit. He died in Nara in 760, and he is buried there.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the first Indian known by name in Japanese history.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thousands held the strings of one Indian monk's brush.

spotlights.name: Okakura Kakuzo and Tagore
spotlights.spot_it: A Japanese scholar in a kimono and a white-bearded Bengali poet, linked by a single phrase: 'Asia is one'.
spotlights.story_md: **Okakura Kakuzo**, an art critic who led the fight to protect Japanese art in the Meiji era, spent much of 1902 in Calcutta with the **Tagore** family. His book *The Ideals of the East* (1903) opens with the line 'Asia is one'. In 1906 he wrote *The Book of Tea* in English, still in print. Japanese painters he sent to Calcutta worked with the Bengal School and shared wash techniques. Rabindranath Tagore made the first of five visits to Japan in **1916**, admired its arts, and publicly warned it against copying Western nationalism.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the cultural friendship behind the later political one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Asia is one: a Japanese wrote it after a year in Kolkata.

spotlights.name: Rash Behari Bose and the curry of Nakamuraya
spotlights.native_name: ラス・ビハリ・ボース
spotlights.spot_it: A plate of Indian-style chicken curry with rice served in a Shinjuku restaurant founded by a bakery family.
spotlights.story_md: **Rash Behari Bose** helped plan the 1912 bomb attack on the Viceroy, Lord Hardinge, in Delhi, and fled to Japan in **1915**. When the British demanded his arrest, the owners of the **Nakamuraya** bakery in Shinjuku, Aizo and Kokko Soma, hid him. He married their daughter Toshiko in 1918 and became a Japanese citizen in 1923. Nakamuraya later served his Indian-style curry, which is still on its menu. In 1942 he helped found the Indian Independence League and handed the movement to **Subhas Chandra Bose**. He died in Tokyo in January 1945.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He links a Tokyo bakery to India's independence struggle.
spotlights.memory_hook: A revolutionary hid in a bakery and left behind a curry.

spotlights.name: Justice Radhabinod Pal
spotlights.native_name: ラダ・ビノード・パール
spotlights.spot_it: A stone memorial with an Indian judge's portrait in a Tokyo shrine garden, often visited by Japanese politicians.
spotlights.story_md: **Radhabinod Pal**, a Bengali jurist, was one of 11 judges at the Tokyo war crimes trial from 1946. He was the only one to find **all** the defendants not guilty, in a dissent of **1,235 pages**. He did not deny Japanese atrocities, which he called overwhelmingly proven. He argued that the charges were invented after the fact and that the trial was victor's justice that ignored the Allies' own bombing of civilians. Japanese nationalists later embraced his dissent. Memorials to him stand at Yasukuni and in Kyoto, and Prime Minister Shinzo Abe met his son in Kolkata in 2007.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is why many Japanese know one Indian name, and why that name is controversial.
spotlights.memory_hook: One judge in eleven said not guilty, to everyone.

spotlights.name: The Maruti 800
spotlights.spot_it: A small white hatchback with square headlights, the car on every Indian street of the 1990s.
spotlights.story_md: In the early 1980s the Indian government's new car company, **Maruti Udyog**, chose a small partner, **Suzuki**, after bigger carmakers lost interest. On **14 December 1983** Prime Minister Indira Gandhi handed the keys of the first **Maruti 800**, based on the Suzuki Alto, to Harpal Singh, who had won a lucky draw. About 2.66 million were sold in India before production ended in 2014. Suzuki brought Japanese factory habits to Gurgaon: shared canteens, the same uniforms for managers and workers, and suppliers clustered nearby. Maruti Suzuki is still India's largest carmaker.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It put India on wheels and planted Japanese manufacturing methods in Indian industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: One lucky draw, 2.66 million cars.

spotlights.name: India's bullet train
spotlights.native_name: ムンバイ・アーメダバード高速鉄道
spotlights.spot_it: Long concrete viaducts striding across Gujarat fields, built to carry Japanese Shinkansen trains.
spotlights.story_md: India's first high-speed line, from **Mumbai to Ahmedabad**, is being built with Shinkansen technology and a Japanese loan that covers more than four-fifths of the cost at 0.1% interest. The line is **508 km** long with 12 stations, including a 7 km tunnel under Thane Creek, and is designed for speeds up to 320 km/h. The foundation stone was laid in 2017 by Narendra Modi and Shinzo Abe. The first section, Surat to Bilimora, is planned to open in **2027** and the full line in 2029. Japan's new **E10** Shinkansen is listed among the trains for the route.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest single project of the India-Japan partnership.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mumbai to Ahmedabad on a Japanese train, on a 0.1% loan.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
A few myths worth correcting:

Geisha are not and were not prostitutes. Ninja did not wear black pyjamas; that look came from stage hands in kabuki, who wear black so the audience ignores them. Japanese people do not eat sushi every day; it is a treat. The idea that the Japanese work the longest hours in the world is out of date: average hours per worker are now below the OECD average, though long unpaid overtime at big firms is real. 'Japan banned all guns' is not quite right either: hunting rifles and shotguns are legal under very strict licensing, and gun deaths are among the lowest in the world.

And some stories that sound like myths are true. A dog really did wait nearly ten years at a station for a master who had died.

spotlights.name: Geisha
spotlights.spot_it: A young woman with white face makeup, red lips, a tall hairstyle with hanging ornaments and a long trailing obi: a maiko, an apprentice.
spotlights.story_md: The word means 'person of the arts'. The first geisha, in the early 18th century, were **men** who entertained at parties with songs and jokes. Women took over from about the **1750s** and soon outnumbered them. Geisha train for years in dance, the three-stringed *shamisen*, singing and conversation; in Kyoto they are called *geiko*, and apprentices *maiko*. The idea that they were prostitutes mixes them up with courtesans, a different, licensed class. Before the Second World War Japan had perhaps 80,000 geisha. Today it has only a few hundred to a thousand or so.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of an outsider's myth about Japan that the facts overturn.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first geisha were men.

spotlights.name: Hachiko
spotlights.spot_it: A small bronze statue of a sitting Akita dog with one ear bent, surrounded by people waiting to meet friends.
spotlights.story_md: **Hachiko**, a white Akita, belonged to **Hidesaburo Ueno**, an agriculture professor who took the train from Shibuya each day. In May 1925 Ueno died suddenly at work. For the next **nine and a half years** the dog came to Shibuya Station every evening at the time his train used to arrive. Newspapers made him famous, and a bronze statue was unveiled in **1934** while he was still alive. He died in March 1935. The first statue was melted for the war effort; the present one dates from 1948. His stuffed body is in Tokyo's National Museum of Nature and Science.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It became Japan's favourite story of loyalty, and Shibuya's meeting point.
spotlights.memory_hook: He had a statue while he was still alive.

sections.title: Japan in 2025 and 2026
sections.intro_md:
**October 2025:** Sanae Takaichi became Japan's first woman Prime Minister on 21 October, after the LDP's 26-year coalition with Komeito broke up and she formed a new one with the Japan Innovation Party.

**November 2025:** Her remark in parliament that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could be an 'existential crisis situation' for Japan set off a long diplomatic row with China.

**8 February 2026:** In a snap election she called, the LDP won **316 of 465** seats, a landslide and a two-thirds majority with its partner.

**2025:** Japan received a record **42.7 million** foreign visitors. Births fell to a new low of **671,236**. Rice prices doubled, and the government released emergency stockpiles.

**June 2026:** The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to about 1%, the highest since 1995, as inflation stuck above target.

**September 2026:** Centenarians passed 100,000 for the first time.

spotlights.name: Sanae Takaichi
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a dark suit at the prime minister's podium, often described as the political heir of Shinzo Abe.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Nara in 1961, **Sanae Takaichi** played drums in a heavy-metal band at university, worked as a TV presenter, and entered parliament in 1993. A conservative and an admirer of Margaret Thatcher, she won the LDP leadership on 4 October 2025 and became Prime Minister on **21 October**, the first woman to hold the post. She called a snap election for 8 February 2026, which gave the LDP 316 of 465 seats, a landslide. Her government has kept the male-only rule for imperial succession and taken a firmer line on China.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the first woman to lead Japan, and one of its most conservative leaders.
spotlights.memory_hook: A heavy-metal drummer became Japan's first woman PM.

spotlights.name: Expo 2025 Osaka
spotlights.spot_it: A giant ring of timber beams two kilometres around, with a walkway on top and pavilions inside.
spotlights.story_md: Osaka hosted the world's fair for the second time (after 1970) on an artificial island, Yumeshima. Its centre was the **Grand Ring** by architect **Sou Fujimoto**: a circle of Japanese cedar and cypress beams joined with traditional techniques, certified by Guinness as the world's largest wooden architectural structure, at about 61,000 m². The Expo drew **29 million** visits over six months. Its blob-like red-and-blue mascot, **Myaku-Myaku**, was mocked at first and then became a best-selling character.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed Japan's bet on timber construction and gave the country a much-needed public success.
spotlights.memory_hook: The biggest wooden building on Earth, made to be taken down.

spotlights.name: Too many visitors
spotlights.spot_it: A convenience store with Mount Fuji rising directly behind it, and a crowd of phones pointed across the road.
spotlights.story_md: Tourism is now one of Japan's top earners, but some places are overwhelmed. In **May 2024** the town of Fujikawaguchiko put up a black mesh screen to block a famous view of Mount Fuji rising behind a Lawson convenience store, because crowds were blocking traffic and trespassing. Yamanashi capped Fuji climbers at 4,000 a day. Residents of Kyoto's Gion asked visitors to stop chasing geisha for photos. Japan's next debate is how to spread visitors around the country rather than turn them away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the cost of Japan's tourism boom, and a test of how a polite society says no.
spotlights.memory_hook: A town built a screen to hide Mount Fuji.

sections.title: Recap: Japan in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. A 3,000 km arc of 14,125 islands on four tectonic plates, three-quarters mountain, with Fuji at 3,776 m.
2. About 123 million people, 29.4% aged 65 or older, and roughly 918,000 more deaths than births a year.
3. Jomon potters made vessels 16,500 years ago, before farming.
4. From 1185 to 1868 shoguns held power while emperors reigned; Tokugawa peace lasted 265 years.
5. Closed from the 1630s, forced open by Perry in 1853, modernised in a generation after 1868.
6. Three scripts, ordered on a Sanskrit pattern; Shinto and Buddhism practised together.
7. Noh, kabuki, the Great Wave, the sword, kintsugi and washi: arts that value pause, wear and repair.
8. Sushi was street food, ramen came from China, instant noodles from a backyard in 1958.
9. India link: Bodhisena in 752, Okakura and Tagore, Rash Behari Bose's curry, the Maruti 800, a bullet train due in 2027.
10. Now: Takaichi, first woman PM; 42.7 million visitors in 2025; a population that keeps shrinking.

side_dish.title: Why Japan shakes, and how a tsunami grows
side_dish.body_md:
Japan sits where ocean plates dive under continental ones, a process called **subduction**. Off Tohoku, the Pacific plate moves west at about 8 to 9 cm a year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow, and slides under the plate that carries northern Japan.

The two plates do not slide smoothly. Their edges lock together, and the upper plate gets dragged down and squeezed like a bent ruler. For centuries, energy builds up. When the lock finally breaks, the upper plate springs back up and out. In 2011 the sea floor off Tohoku jumped by several metres along a fault hundreds of kilometres long.

That jump lifted the entire column of water above it, from the sea floor to the surface. In the deep ocean, the resulting **tsunami** is only a metre or so high but extremely long, and travels at 700 to 800 km/h, as fast as a jet. Ships at sea barely notice it. As it reaches shallow water near the coast, it slows down, the back of the wave catches up with the front, and the water piles up. That is how a wave a metre high in the open sea becomes a wall of water tens of metres high on land.

This is why Japan's warning system tells coastal people to run uphill as soon as the shaking stops, without waiting to see the sea. The same physics explains the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami that struck Tamil Nadu and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

offline_task.title: Make a ten-minute miso soup with real dashi
offline_task.body_md:
This is the bowl at the centre of washoku, and it teaches you what umami tastes like.

1. Soak a 10 cm piece of dried kelp (kombu) in 600 ml of cold water for 20 minutes, or as long as you have.
2. Heat slowly. Remove the kelp just before the water boils.
3. Add a handful of dried bonito flakes (katsuobushi), turn off the heat, wait two minutes, then strain. This is dashi. Taste it on its own first: that savoury depth is umami. (No bonito? Use two dried shiitake mushrooms soaked with the kelp.)
4. Warm the dashi again, add cubes of soft tofu and a little sliced spring onion or wakame.
5. Turn off the heat. Put 2 to 3 tablespoons of miso paste in a ladle, dip it in the soup and stir to dissolve. Never boil miso; it dulls the flavour.

Drink it from the bowl, holding it with both hands, and eat the tofu with chopsticks. Write one line on how it differs from a dal or a rasam.

best_facts.fact: Japanese hunter-gatherers made pottery about 16,500 years ago, thousands of years before anyone in Japan farmed.
Japan's holiest shrine, Ise Jingu, is torn down and rebuilt every 20 years. The 62nd rebuilding was in 2013.
best_facts.why_surprising: The oldest shrine is always new.

best_facts.fact: The eyes of Nara's Great Buddha were painted in 752 by Bodhisena, a monk from India.
best_facts.why_surprising: An Indian name at the heart of Japan's biggest Buddha.

best_facts.fact: Japan's syllable order, a-i-u-e-o, ka-ki-ku-ke-ko, follows the phonetic order of Sanskrit grammarians.
best_facts.why_surprising: Every Japanese dictionary is arranged on an Indian pattern.

best_facts.fact: Kongo Gumi, a temple builder founded in 578, ran for about 1,400 years through 40 generations before a takeover in 2006.
best_facts.why_surprising: Older than Islam, still in business.

best_facts.fact: Kyoto's cherry blossoms peaked on 26 March 2021, the earliest date in a record kept since 812.
The average Tokaido Shinkansen train ran 0.7 minutes late in fiscal 2018, including typhoons and earthquakes.
best_facts.why_surprising: Under a minute, averaged across disasters.

best_facts.fact: The word kamikaze first meant the typhoon that wrecked Kublai Khan's invasion fleet in 1281.
best_facts.why_surprising: A weather word became a wartime word.

best_facts.fact: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake moved the main island of Honshu about 2.4 m east.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole island moved in an afternoon.

best_facts.fact: The first geisha were men; women took over only from the 1750s.
Modern group taiko drumming was invented in 1951 by a jazz drummer, Daihachi Oguchi.
Japan recorded 671,236 births and 1,589,489 deaths in 2025.
best_facts.why_surprising: More than two deaths for every birth.

best_facts.fact: Radhabinod Pal was the only one of 11 Tokyo trial judges to find every defendant not guilty, in a 1,235-page dissent.
best_facts.why_surprising: An Indian judge is honoured at a Tokyo shrine.

best_facts.fact: Rash Behari Bose, who helped plan the 1912 bomb attack on the Viceroy, hid in a Tokyo bakery and married the owners' daughter.
best_facts.why_surprising: A revolutionary's refuge became a curry restaurant.

best_facts.fact: Hachiko had a bronze statue at Shibuya Station unveiled in 1934, while he was still alive and still waiting.
best_facts.why_surprising: Statues are usually for the dead.

best_facts.fact: Nintendo was founded in 1889 to make playing cards.
best_facts.why_surprising: Mario's company is older than the car.

best_facts.fact: The Mumbai to Ahmedabad bullet train is funded mostly by a Japanese loan at 0.1% interest.
The Great Wave is so cheap a print that thousands were made; since 2024 it is on Japan's 1,000 yen note.
best_facts.why_surprising: A mass-market print became a national symbol.
